references.text: Moses was asked, 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?' (Exod 2:14). Jesus' answer in Luke 12:14 almost word-for-word reflects this question, as he rejects the role of a secular judge, just as Moses was rejected in his role.

The context in Exod 2:13-14 shows the situation where two Hebrews are quarreling and Moses tries to intervene, but is rejected with the question of who made him a judge. Jesus uses similar language to reject a similar role.
In Stephen's speech in Acts 7:27-28, Exodus 2:14 is quoted directly: 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?' This parallel to Moses' rejection sheds light on Jesus' answer in Luke 12:14.

In Acts 7:35, Stephen points out that the Moses who was rejected with the words 'Who made you a ruler and judge?' was precisely sent by God as leader and deliverer. Jesus, who rejects the role of secular judge, is in reality appointed by God as the final judge.

In John 18:36, Jesus says that his kingdom is not of this world. His refusal to act as a judge in an inheritance dispute in Luke 12:14 underscores the same point: his mission did not concern worldly disputes.
In John 8:15, Jesus says, 'You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one.' This parallels Luke 12:14, where Jesus refuses to act as a secular judge between two brothers.

In Matt 22:17-21, Jesus distinguishes between what belongs to Caesar and what belongs to God. Similarly, in Luke 12:14 he declines to interfere in worldly legal disputes, showing that his calling concerns the spiritual kingdom.

In Dan 7:13-14, the Son of Man is given dominion and the kingdom by God. Jesus is appointed as judge by God, but in Luke 12:14 he refuses to be made a judge by humans in a worldly dispute, highlighting the difference between divine and human authority.
